data.name: Gauri
data.long_meaning: Gauri is the Hindu goddess of fertility, marriage, and the wife of Lord Shiva. Her name comes from the Sanskrit word ‘gaur’ which means ‘fair, radiant, or golden’. Gauri is also known as Parvati, the embodiment of love, beauty, and maternal love. She is often depicted as a beautiful, young woman with multiple arms, adorned with flowers and jewels, and holding a trident or a lotus in her hands.
data.spiritual_meaning: Symbol of love, beauty, and maternal protection.

vedic_reference.note: Gauri is the name of the Hindu goddess Parvati, the consort of Lord Shiva. She is the goddess of fertility, love, beauty, and marriage.

data.cultural_impact: Gauri is a revered Hindu goddess and an important deity in Hindu households. She is often invoked during marriage ceremonies and celebrated during the festival of Navratri, specifically on the day dedicated to her, on the fifth day.
data.spiritual_significance: Gauri is believed to be the personification of pure love, compassion, and maternal love. She represents the divine feminine, the shakti or power that creates and sustains the universe. Worship of Gauri is said to grant blessings of prosperity, happiness, love, and fulfillment of desires.

historical_references.reference: Gauri is an epithet of Parvati, the consort of Shiva. According to Hindu mythology, Shiva was once in deep meditation with the goddess Kali standing beside him. Kali, in a fit of anger, tried to destroy the universe, but was calmed by Shiva who opened his third eye to destroy the demon Tripurasura. In his fury, the destruction was too extensive and Parvati intervened to restore balance to the universe. She took on the form of Gauri, the beautiful and calming goddess, and Shiva was so enthralled with her that he agreed to marry her. This event is believed to have occurred prior to the 6th century BC.

Another reference for Gauri is found in the Mahabharata, where she is mentioned as the mother of two of the five Pandava brothers, Bhima and Yudhishthira. In the epic, Bhima, disguised as a Brahmin, approaches Gangotri to offer his obeisance. Gauri, disguised as the goddess, tests Bhima's devotion and strength by asking him to bring the water of the Ganges to her. Bhima, despite the seemingly impossible task, succeeds in bringing the water and is blessed by Gauri. This episode is believed to have occurred in the 4th century BC.
